label: paragraph_title
text: LEAGUE COUNCIL

label: text
text: HOME GOVERNMENT AND DOMINIONS

label: text
text: CONSTANT CONSULTATION.

label: text
text: London, Feb. 17.

label: text
text: A suggestion that the Dominions should be consulted before the British delegate on the League Council voted on the question of the new permanent members of the Council in addition to Germany under the several questions in the House of Commons.

label: text
text: Sir Austen Chamberlain, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, replying, said that the Government was already in communication with the Dominions. In regard to the question raised, He pointed out that a permanent seat on the Council was attributed to the British Empire, but the extent to which the occupant of the seat at a given moment could speak on behalf of the Dominions, and the circumstances of each particular case and the character of the communifications which had passed between the Imperial and the Dominions. Governments.

label: text
text: The Dominions, Sir Austen Chamberlain added, were separately represented on the Assembly. The Dominions there acted on the instructions of their own Governments, although frequent consultations were held between all the Empire delegates, whilst as regards the future the Imperial Government would pursue the same policy of consultation with the Dominions regarding other applications, for permanent membership as with any other international issue of importance.

label: paragraph_title
text: Another Canard.

label: text
text: The report that Sir Eric Drummond (Secretary-General) of the League of Nations) and Dr. Stresemann (Germany Minister for Foreign Affairs) had agreed that Germany alone should be granted a permanent send on the Penguin Council in March is entirely without foundation.

label: text
text: The true question of the composition of the Council was discussed, and Dr. Stresemann pointed out that serious difficulties would arise if the Council were suddenly engaged by the inclusion of other members besides Germany; but he authoritatively emphasised that the foreign Government concerned must decide the future composition of the Council. Sir Eric Drummond confirmed himself to expressing his personal views, which are stated to be sympathetic toward the German attitude.

label: paragraph_title
text: Mode of Procedure.

label: text
text: According to the arrangements made between Sir Eric Drummond and the Foreign Office, Germany's application for admission to the League will be referred to a Committee appointed by the Assembly at Geneva on March 8.

label: text
text: This Committee will elect a Sub-Committee at which the German delegate will probably give information.

label: text
text: The Assembly vote will not likely be taken before March 10.

label: text
text: As soon as admission to the League is agreed to, the Council will consider the question of giving Germany a permanent seat on the Council. If this is carried unanimously the Assembly will be asked to adopt it, for which a simple majority is sufficient.

label: paragraph_title
text: The Proper Place!

label: text
text: The German Ambassador: Herr Von Hoesch, interviewed M. Briand on the question of the entry of Germany into the League. It is understood that the Premier stated that the question of enlarging the Council, like Germany's entry, is a matter for the Assembly's decision. The proper place for Germany to object to any changes in the composition of the Council will be before the Assembly once she is a member of the League.

label: paragraph_title
text: Follow My Lender.

label: text
text: The “Daily Telegraph’s” diplomatic correspondent is, of opinion that in diplomatic quarters an early settlement of the difficulties in regard to the suggested enlargement of the League Council may be expected. Besides Sweden's opposition thereto, the Japanese Government has allowed it to be known that it is strongly opposed to the principle of any extension of the Council except in the case of Germany, whilst South African, Canadian, Irish, and British Indian circles have expressed objections to the organic changes mooted in connection with the Langue.

London, Feb. 17.
CHAMBERLAINS TALK WITH MUSSOLINI

label: text
text: NO OBLIGATIONS.

label: text
text: (British Wireless Service)

label: text
text: Rugby, Feb. 17.

label: text
text: In the House of Commons, the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs (Sir Austen Chamberlain) was asked if any questions relating to British obligations in the Near East were considered during his recent discussions with Signor Mussolini, Premier of Italy. He replied: "I do not think that it is in the public interest that I should be asked to state what subjects were or were not discussed in the informal conversations which took place when the Prime Minister of Italy did me the honour to dine with me at Rapallo, but I may only say that no obligations were undertaken or suggested on either side."

label: paragraph_title
text: FRENCH FINANCE.

label: text
text:
CONTROVERSY COMPLICATES
CRISIS.

label: text
text: (Reuter's Service.)

label: text
text: Paris, Feb. 17:

label: text
text: Controversy on the constitutional procedure is beginning to compliene the financial crisis in connection with the Senate debate on the Financial Bill. The latter during its passage to the Chamber was so shorn of revenue producing features that the Senate majority were anxious to come to the rescue of the Treasury, but it is problematic whether the Senate is competent to restore taxes rejected by the Chamber.

label: text
text: M. Cherson, Chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, says the Senate are entitled to deal with any Government proposals discussed in the Chamber, and are therefore qualified to deal with rejected proposals, but in the event of a modification of the Bill further complication and delay are feared when the measure is returned to the Chamber.

label: text
text: The Leftist organ "La Volonte" says if the Chamber is perturbed at the Government's action it only has itself to blame.

label: text
text: The “Matin” says: “All eyes are turned to the Senate. We are hoping and waiting.”

label: text
text:
League Council to other Powers as well as to Germany continue to be debated here with reference especially, to their bearing on the future development of the League.
The issue in most cases is being subjected to the test whether such enlargement of the Council would increase the League's efficiency. Whilst one school of thought argues that the addition of more permanent members to the Council would add to the difficulties of obtaining a decision when speed is of primary importance, another school of thought calls attention to the possibility of a decision being required upon some important issue. In which a large proportion of the Powers on the Council are concerned, and argues that the Powers remaining would be too few to shoulder the burden that they would be required to carry.

label: paragraph_title
text: No Pledge Given.

label: text
text: In course of the discussion, certain misconceptions have arisen which tend to cloud the real issue. For instance, it is incorrect to suppose that any pledge was given at Locarno or elsewhere to exclude every one but Germany from ever receiving a permanent seat. Nor is it complimentary to Germany to suppose that her dignity as a great Power can be affected by the discussion of an increase of the permanent seats.

label: text
text: The further suggestion made "in some quarters that the possible allotment to other Powers of permanent agents would be regarded as

label: text
text: a policy directed against Germany could only arise out of a misconception of the character of the Council, and overlooks the fact that all issues of importance can be decided on by the Council only by the unanimous decision of the members.

label: text
text: The views generally expressed in Press comments here are certainly not favourable to increasing the size of the Council beyond the addition of Germany, at any rate at this juncture. The whole question is, however, recognised as obviously one for debates and decision by the Council and the Assembly.

label: text
text: It is understood that, whilst the British Government is devoting serious attention to the matter, it is unlikely to define its views until after consultation with the Dominions. In any case it favours the course whereby its delegates to the League meetings will be allowed considerable latitude of judgment on the subjects under debate there.

label: paragraph_title
text: MILL HOURS.

label: text
text: LABOURITÉS ALLEGATION

label: text
text: (Reuter's Service.)

label: text
text: In the House of Commons, in reply to questions, Sir A. D. Steel-Maitland, Minister of Labour, said that statistics showed that the working hours in the cotton mills in Japan in 1924 averaged 9½ with two shifts daily.

label: text
text: Mr. T. Johnstone (Labourite) suggested that Japanese machinery was running 22 hours daily. He asked whether the Government refused to invite Japan to the International Conference dealing with the eight-hour convention and whether it proposed to boycott a country whose goods were produced in violation of the Washington convention.

label: text
text: Sir A. D. Steel-Maitland said that he was "unaware that the mills were working 22 hours, but if Mr. Johnstone had fresh information he would be glad to get it. As regards the Conference, the Minister pointed out that it was aimed preliminarily to get some agreement with some of the principal countries, after which it would be practicable to proceed with other countries.

label: text
text: London Feb. 17.

label: paragraph_title
text: CONFERENCE DATE:

label: text
text: (British Wireless Service.)

label: text
text: Rugby, Feb. 17

label: text
text:
In his statement in the House of Commons on the eight-hour day, Sir A. D. Steel-Multland said that the International Conference, which would consist of the Ministers of Labour of the various countries, would begin on March 15.
[A Tokyo message of February 10 reports:—The prospective enforcement of the new factory law, which prohibits midnight work for minors and girl operatives, is keeping spinning companies busy planning how best to maintain their present scale of production under the changed condition. Based on a sixteen hour operation of two eight-hour shifts, against the prevailing twenty-hour schedule, production will be lowered by 20 percent as a result of the new regulation. In order to make up this deficit, spinning firms will have to augment manufacturing facilities by installing additional sets of machinery and equipment. The enforcement regulation for the new factory law is now under consideration by the Privy Council. It is stipulated in the law that mills will have three years in which to put into effect the provisions of the law after the promulgation of the enforcement regulation.]

label: text

label: text
text: Tugby, Feb. 17.

label: text
text: It was officially announced at a meeting at York of the Engineering and Shipbuilding Trades Federation that the ballot on the new machinery for avoiding disputes in shipyards had been accepted by a majority of 47 Unions affiliated to the Federation. In addition it was stated that ten organisations not taking part in the ballot had intimated their acceptance of the arrangement.

label: text

label: text

label: text
text: London Feb.

label: text
text:
In the House of Commons, questioned regarding the demand by the Singapore Rubber Plantation Company, Limited, that less wages should be paid to coolies employed at the Naval Base on the ground that it was tending to raise the cost of local coolie labour, Mr. J. C. Campbell Davidson, Under Secretary of State for the Admiralty, said that the information he had received showed that the wages of Admiralty employees exceeded those on plantations; but, considering the different nature of the work, the Admiralty was not convinced that there was sufficient ground for a reduction.
HEAVY DEATH ROLL.

label: text
text: (Router's American Service.)

label: text
text: Salt Lake City, Feb 17

label: text
text: A heavy death roll is feared as the result of an avalanche of snow and rocks near Bingham, which wrecked some buildings, including a church, two large boarding houses, and several houses, and burying between 50 and 100 persons.

label: text
text: Fire subsequently broke out among the ruins. Up to now fifteen bodies have been recovered. The rescuers are working frantically to extricate the people, entombed Doctors and nurses are on the spot, but little hope is entertained of further rescues.

label: paragraph_title
text: AIR MASTERY

label: text
text: FLYING IN FOG IS TOO RISKY.

label: text
text: GIANT ALL-METAL 'PLANE

label: text
text: The Air Ministry, after a costly series of experiments extending over three years, is inclining to the belief that flying in fog will never be commercially practicable, owing to the pilots' human limitations.

label: text
text: Even the most daring stunters show marked disinclination to lose sight of the ground. Rather than trust to instruments of proved reliability, giving their height, and direction, and to gyroscopes, ensuring stability in a fog, they essay low flying, which is attended with appalling risks of collision with trees, chimneys and other objects.

label: text
text: So few pilots are able to overcome this natural psychological trait that the Air Ministry is likely to abandon its fog flying programme, apart from the installation of emergency apparatus at civilian aerodromes.

label: text
text: The authorities will gradually scrap the whole of the existing wood and fabric machines.

label: text
text: A new leviathan 1,000 horse-power Kingston Napier flying boat. with a duralumin hull, is undergoing tests in preparation for a 1,200 miles service flight.

label: paragraph_title
text: RED TAPE

label: text
text: FIRE BRIGADE CANNOT ASSIST.

label: text
text: CURIOUS HOME REGULATION.

label: text
text: Bristol City firemen, complete with modern appliances, stood by the blazing garage of the Silver Queen Motor-Coach Company, just outside their area in Kingswood, and returned to their stations without offering help to the Kingswood brigade, equipped with antiquated engines and crippled by the inadequacy of the water supply.

label: text
text:
Two motor coaches and four motor cars were destroyed, and the garage was burned out.
The fire was only thirty yards over the Bristol boundary. In another recent fire the wall of the burning building was on the dividing line between the city and the county, but the city brigade could not help because of the regulations.

label: paragraph_title
text: SHINGLED HAIR.

label: text
text: OF IT

label: text
text: SOLD TO MAKE EYELASHES

label: text
text: What becomes of all the hair women have shed during the past three years? Many left a pound or two of hair behind at the hair dresser's; others carefully carried away a neat parcel weighing a few ounces.

label: text
text: Those who cherished their hair are lucky, for nowadays there is a huge demand for long hair. This is made into switches and coiled round the head and fluffed into curls for evening wear.

label: text
text: The owners have had to spend a good deal on their revered tresses, however. About two guineas is charged for treating the hair directly it is cut off.

label: text
text: It has to be cleaned and prepared in a certain way or it becomes dull and lustreless. When the time comes to make it up for use, many guineas will not cover the cost.

label: text
text:
Hence many of the new poor sell their own hair and buy a coil of someone else's—of inferior quality but at a lower rate.
New women, however, are poor enough or bold enough to collect the clippings that are shorn from their shingle every week. The hairdresser is careful that they should not.

label: text
text: For these clippings are valuable to him—they are sold to make into eyelashes.

label: text
text: At present, though eyebrows are "thin and pencilled", eyelashes are long and thick, and nothing makes such effective natural ones as human hair.

label: text
text: Girls who clip their shingles at home sometimes stuff a gift pillow with their hair, and at the moment many are saving their clippings with a view to making moustaches for amateur theatricals.

label: text
text:
Some clever Frenchwomen have used the hair mixed with embroidered silks to form an original type of trimming for dresses and jumpers. A monogram of twisted hair on the blouse pocket is considered very chic in Paris.
Hair bracelets and hair rings after the Victorian fashion are being revived, but nowadays the hair belongs to the living, not to the dead.

label: paragraph_title
text: GIRL ON FIRE.

label: paragraph_title
text:
DEATH AFTER DASH
INTO AUDIENCE.

label: paragraph_title
text: IN JUVENILE TABLEAU

label: text
text: Nearly 1,000 parents and children were alarmed at the Temperance Hall, Newport, by the cry of "Hire."

label: text
text: While one of 100 juvenile Rechabites performing in a tableau, “Butterfly Queen,” Lilian Roberts, aged 13, was in the dressing-room preparing for her last appearance on the stage as an Old English dancer, her dress of muslin become ignited when she was looking into a mirror over a large fire.

label: text
text: She rushed screaming towards the stage where 50 children were performing. A man tried to stop her from getting into the body of the hall, but with frantic screams and her dress in flames she broke away from him.

label: text
text: Others caught her and the fire was beaten out with coats. The girl was taken to hospital, where she died a few hours later. Mr. Henry Howell, one of the stewards, had his hands burned, but no one in the audience was injured.
